facts.claim: A Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas, because local authorities may ask you to prove you are not already married. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices across Australia, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.reused_from: destination-wedding-in-vietnam B F-100 (originally greece-marriage-licence B F-100, read 2026-11-12)
facts.use_note: For Malta: DFAT in Australia can issue the CNI. Whether the Australian High Commission in Malta issues CNIs in person was NOT confirmed on its own site (N-100); DFAT says high commissions generally can.

facts.claim: At least one person applying for the CNI must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident. Supporting documents: Australian citizen, a valid Australian passport; permanent resident, a valid foreign passport with evidence of permanent residence; foreign citizen partner, a valid foreign passport or photo ID; divorced, a Divorce Certificate; widowed, the deceased partner's Death Certificate. Originals or certified true copies; non-English documents need a professional English translation.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: How to apply for a CNI through DFAT: complete the CNI application form, signing it only in front of an authorised witness (in Australia a Justice of the Peace, or an Australian Passports official at your appointment; overseas a consular official). If the overseas authority wants documents legalised, also complete a Document Legalisation Request Form. Submit by mail or in person and pay on submission. Incomplete applications are not processed. DFAT advises checking whether the CNI must be issued in the country of marriage, in which case the Australian embassy there can issue it.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Whether Malta's Marriage Registry wants the CNI apostilled is a Malta-side question (N-101).

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026, in Australian dollars: Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage AUD 181; document legalisation by Apostille AUD 105. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year.
facts.use_note: Write 'AUD 181 per CNI (2026 fee)' and 'AUD 105 per apostille (2026 fee)'. Re-check after 1 January 2027.

facts.claim: DFAT does not publish a fixed processing time for legalisation: 'Processing times vary', with delays at the end of the school year and during peak holiday periods, when a request is incomplete or unpaid, or when DFAT must contact the document's issuing authority.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get your documents legalised

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where either person was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but may not be usable as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory BDM registry. Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm an overseas certificate is valid in Australia.

The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a change of name. Legal basis: Marriage Act 1961, Part VA (recognition of foreign marriages).
facts.use_note: Cite Part VA by name only; section text not read.

facts.claim: Passport name change after marriage: for a new passport you must link the new name to your Australian birth or citizenship certificate with an Australian RBDM marriage certificate, registered relationship certificate, or RBDM name change certificate. The Passport Office always requires an RBDM name change certificate if you were born in Australia and married overseas. Foreign certificates are accepted only if you cannot get an Australian equivalent, must be legalised, and non-English documents must be translated in full by an approved translation service.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office, Change of name or gender
facts.use_note: An Australian-born spouse married in Malta first registers a change of name with their state BDM before a passport in the new name. Language of Maltese marriage certificates not checked (N-102).

facts.claim: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages: a person legally married in Australia can take their spouse's family name without registering a change of name (the exemption is worded for marriages in Australia). Foreign documents not in English must be translated in full and stamped by a NAATI-accredited translator, with copies of the original and the translation.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
facts.use_note: NSW only; other states not checked.

facts.claim: If you change your family name because of marriage, you can choose to get a new passport or keep using your current one, and the Australian Passport Office recommends booking travel in the name that is in your passport.
facts.use_note: Book the honeymoon in the name on the passport you will carry.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's essentials checklist says to confirm your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond the end of your trip; some countries and some airlines apply a six-month validity rule, it can apply when transiting, and getting it wrong can mean being stranded.
facts.use_note: The Malta page today says 'Many countries' (F-119). Safe wording: 'check your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond your trip'.

facts.claim: Allow at least 6 weeks to get a passport; where possible, don't book flights without a valid passport; faster processing may be available for urgent travel at an extra fee.

Legal at home, celebration abroad: Australia has no marriage licence; the formal step is giving a Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM) to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. You do not have to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident to marry in Australia. Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM can be witnessed remotely by audio-visual link, and a couple outside Australia can complete it with an authorised witness overseas (such as an Australian consular officer or a notary public, not a celebrant).
facts.reused_from: getting-married-in-france B F-112 (originally marriage-licence-requirements A F-001 to F-005)

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage, and must be physically present to solemnise it, together with the couple and 2 witnesses over 18. There are no video-link weddings.
facts.use_note: The legal ceremony must happen in Australia with the celebrant present; it cannot be done from Malta by video.

facts.claim: After an Australian ceremony the celebrant must submit the NOIM, the Declaration of No Legal Impediment and the Official Certificate of Marriage to the BDM registry in the state or territory where the marriage took place within 14 days.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Benefit of the home route: an Australian BDM certificate, which the Passport Office accepts directly (F-107).

facts.claim: HCCH status table for the 1961 Apostille Convention (last update 30 June 2026): Malta acceded on 12 June 1967 and the Convention entered into force for Malta on 3 March 1968 (type A, accession, no objection marker); Australia has been a party since 16 March 1995. Both are Contracting Parties, so an Australian public document for use in Malta is legalised by apostille rather than consular legalisation.
facts.publisher: Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH), Apostille Convention status table
facts.use_note: Apostille from DFAT (AUD 105 per document, 2026 fee, F-103). Which Australian documents Malta's Marriage Registry wants apostilled is a Malta-side question (N-101). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Malta: Malta is part of the Schengen area. Australians can travel without a visa to the Schengen area, including Malta, for up to 90 days in any 180-day period as a tourist, to visit family or friends, for business meetings, cultural or sports events, or short-term study; total Schengen stay must not exceed this limit. For a short stay on an Australian passport you must have fingerprints and photo taken and answer Schengen Border Code questions under the EU Entry/Exit System (EES) on arrival; EES is free, needs no action before arrival, and may cause border delays. Entry conditions can change at short notice; contact the High Commission of Malta for visa details.
facts.use_note: Page still current at 17 November 2026, updated 7 October 2026. A wedding trip counts as a tourist or family visit; do not state it as a named visa-free category. The 90 days is across the whole Schengen area, so a Malta wedding plus a Europe honeymoon shares one allowance. Warn readers about fraudulent EES and ETIAS sites.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Malta: ETIAS is separate from EES; there is no confirmed implementation date, the EU will announce it several months before launch, and applications are not yet open. Once implemented, visa-free visitors to the 30 participating countries will need an ETIAS authorisation before travel. Dual citizens of a participating country will have to enter on that country's passport, not their Australian one.
facts.use_note: Relevant for Maltese-Australian dual citizens (common in this audience): once ETIAS starts they enter on the Maltese passport. Smartraveller also says Malta recognises dual nationality with no military or civil service obligations.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's overall advice for Malta is 'Exercise normal safety precautions' (still current at 17 November 2026; updated 7 October 2026). For consular help contact the Australian High Commission, Ta' Xbiex Terrace, Ta' Xbiex; telephone +356 2133 8201; email consular.malta@dfat.gov.au; website malta.highcommission.gov.au. The 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre is +61 2 6261 3305 from overseas.
facts.use_note: Point readers to the High Commission to ask whether it issues CNIs in person in Malta (N-100). Advice levels can change; link the page.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Malta passport note: many countries require your passport to be valid for at least 6 months before entering or departing, including for transit; the Australian Government does not make these rules.
facts.use_note: Generic wording, not a Malta-specific rule; it says 'many' where the essentials checklist says 'some' (F-110). Do not state a Malta six-month rule as fact.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Malta local travel: ferries link Cirkewwa and Gozo, Valletta and Gozo (fast ferry), and other routes; weather can cause cancellations or delays, particularly on ferry lines to and from Gozo, and summer schedules differ from a reduced winter service on some routes. Roads can be narrow, congested and prone to flash flooding in heavy rain. Hunting with firearms is common in rural Malta: the spring season is in April (dates announced each March) and the autumn season usually runs 1 September to 31 January.
facts.use_note: Only weather-related notes Smartraveller gives; it does not state monthly climate. For a Gozo wedding, build ferry buffer into guest travel. Hunting note is for rural outdoor venues only; keep it light.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Malta: Australia and Malta have a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement covering you for up to 6 months after arrival at public facilities; it does not cover private facilities or ongoing treatment of existing conditions and does not replace travel insurance. Malta's currency is the euro; you must declare 10,000 euros or more when entering, transiting or leaving.
facts.use_note: Optional travel-prep line. The cash declaration matters only for couples carrying vendor payments in cash.

legal.summary: DFAT issues CNIs in Australia, by mail and through overseas missions. The Australian High Commission Malta's own CNI process was not found on its website; confirm with the High Commission (consular.malta@dfat.gov.au). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.

Both parties to the Apostille Convention (Malta since 3 March 1968, Australia since 16 March 1995): Australian documents for Malta are apostilled by DFAT. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process with Malta's Marriage Registry.
No Australian registration of overseas marriages; generally recognised if valid in Malta and would be valid in Australia (Marriage Act 1961, Part VA). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Passport in married name: Australian-born spouse married overseas needs an RBDM name change certificate. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Legal at home route: NOIM to an authorised celebrant 1 to 18 months ahead; celebrant physically present. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
